title: What is an `enum` in Java, and how can it have fields, constructors, and methods?
shortTitle: What is an enum in Java, and how can it have fields, constructors, and methods?

s1_definition.profdef: An `enum` in Java is a special reference type that represents a fixed, finite set of named constant instances. Each constant is a singleton object of the enum type, created once by the JVM at class load time. Because an enum is a full class under the hood (it implicitly extends `java.lang.Enum`), it can declare instance fields, constructors, and methods, so each constant can carry its own data and behavior.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, an account can only ever be in one of a small set of known states: ACTIVE, FROZEN, or CLOSED. It would be dangerous to store this as a raw String like "active" or "Activ" because a typo would silently break the system. An enum is like a sealed stamp drawer with exactly three labelled stamps. Rajesh's savings account (SAV2001) can be stamped ACTIVE and Priya's current account (CUR3001) can be stamped FROZEN, but nobody can invent a fourth stamp at runtime. Each stamp can also carry extra printed information, like a description and whether withdrawals are allowed.
s1_definition.oneliner: An enum is a type-safe, fixed set of singleton constants that can each hold fields and behavior like a real class.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An `enum` in Java is a special reference type that represents a fixed, finite set of named constant instances. Each constant is a singleton object of the enum type, created once by the JVM at class load time. Because an enum is a full class under the hood (it implicitly extends `java.lang.Enum`), it can declare instance fields, constructors, and methods, so each constant can carry its own data and behavior.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, an account can only ever be in one of a small set of known states: ACTIVE, FROZEN, or CLOSED. It would be dangerous to store this as a raw String like "active" or "Activ" because a typo would silently break the system. An enum is like a sealed stamp drawer with exactly three labelled stamps. Rajesh's savings account (SAV2001) can be stamped ACTIVE and Priya's current account (CUR3001) can be stamped FROZEN, but nobody can invent a fourth stamp at runtime. Each stamp can also carry extra printed information, like a description and whether withdrawals are allowed.

**One line to remember:** An enum is a type-safe, fixed set of singleton constants that can each hold fields and behavior like a real class.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India stores the state of every account. In the early days a junior developer stored this state as a plain String column, writing values like "active", "ACTIVE", and even "frozen " with a trailing space. When the withdrawal service checked `if (status.equals("ACTIVE"))`, Priya's genuinely frozen account slipped through because its status had been saved as "Frozen" with different casing, and money was almost released. This is exactly the problem an enum solves, because an enum makes the set of allowed values a closed list the compiler enforces, so an invalid state cannot even be typed.

Problem 2 — The bank needs each status to carry extra rules, not just a name. A frozen account must block withdrawals, an active account must allow them, and a closed account must block everything and show a clear message to the customer. Putting this logic in scattered if-statements across the codebase is fragile. This is exactly how an enum with fields and methods works, because each constant stores its own `withdrawAllowed` flag and its own display label, so the rule lives next to the constant and every part of the system asks the same single source of truth.

In the mini-project we build a small withdrawal check. We define the `AccountStatus` enum with a label and a withdraw flag. We define an `Account` class with accountId, holderName, balance, a status, and `debit` and `credit` methods. We define a `WithdrawalService` that reads the account status and decides whether Rajesh or Priya may withdraw. The demo creates Rajesh (SAV2001, 1000000, ACTIVE) and Priya (CUR3001, 250000, FROZEN), attempts a withdrawal on each, and logs the outcome. The code will show enum fields, the enum constructor, an enum method `canWithdraw()`, and safe `==` comparison.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, balance 1000000, status ACTIVE) withdrawing 50000, and Priya (CUR3001, balance 250000, status FROZEN) withdrawing 10000.

Step 1: At class load time the JVM creates the three AccountStatus singletons once. ACTIVE stores label "Active account" and withdrawAllowed true, FROZEN stores "Frozen by compliance" and false, CLOSED stores "Closed permanently" and false. These objects now exist for the whole program life.

Step 2: The demo builds two Account objects. Rajesh holds a reference to the single ACTIVE constant, and Priya holds a reference to the single FROZEN constant. No copies are made; both point to shared singletons.

Step 3: WithdrawalService.withdraw runs for Rajesh. It calls `rajesh.getStatus().canWithdraw()`, which reads the withdrawAllowed field on the ACTIVE constant and returns true. The balance check passes because 1000000 is greater than 50000, so debit runs and the balance becomes 950000.

Step 4: WithdrawalService.withdraw runs for Priya. It calls `priya.getStatus().canWithdraw()`, which reads the withdrawAllowed field on the FROZEN constant and returns false. The method logs a BLOCKED warning using the frozen label and returns immediately. Priya's balance stays 250000, unchanged.

Step 5: The demo logs the total number of statuses using `values().length`, which is three, and confirms `priya.getStatus() == AccountStatus.FROZEN` is true using a fast reference comparison.

```text
[INFO] SUCCESS: Rajesh withdrew Rs.50000, new balance Rs.950000
[WARNING] BLOCKED: Priya account CUR3001 is Frozen by compliance
[INFO] Total declared statuses: 3
[INFO] Is priya frozen? true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An enum in Java is a special reference type that defines a fixed, finite set of named constants, where each constant is a singleton instance created once by the JVM when the enum class is loaded. Although it looks like a simple list of names, under the hood an enum is a full class that implicitly extends java.lang.Enum, which is exactly why it can declare instance fields, a constructor, and methods just like any ordinary class.

The way fields and constructors work is that each constant calls the enum's constructor with its own arguments, so each constant can carry its own data. The constructor is always effectively private, which is what guarantees nobody can create a new value at runtime and the set stays closed. In my banking work I use this constantly for account status, where I define ACTIVE, FROZEN, and CLOSED, and each constant stores a human-readable label and a boolean saying whether withdrawals are allowed, exposed through a canWithdraw method.

The practical benefit is type safety and keeping rules next to the data. Before we used enums, status was a plain String, and a casing mismatch once nearly let a frozen account release money. With an enum the compiler rejects any invalid value, and because each constant is a singleton I compare with double equals, which is faster and null-safe compared to String equals. I also attach behavior directly, so the withdrawal rule lives inside the status itself rather than being copied into scattered if-statements across the codebase.

One senior nuance I always mention is persistence. I store the enum's name, never its ordinal, in the database, because ordinal is just the declaration position and reordering the constants later would silently corrupt every stored record. So my complete answer is that an enum is a type-safe fixed set of singleton constants that can hold fields, constructors, and methods, giving me compiler-enforced valid values, safe reference comparison, thread safety, and behavior that lives right next to the data it governs.
